questions.prompt: Nonempty pairwise disjoint subsets Aₙ of ℤ, n≥1, have union ℤ. Which necessarily hold?

options.D: Every Aₙ is countable, finite or infinite

hints: Every Aₙ is a subset of ℤ.
Compare a singleton partition with the rows of a bijection ℕ²→ℤ.
questions.solution: Every subset of the countable set ℤ is at most countable, giving D. A and B fail for a partition into infinitely many infinite sets: choose a bijection ℕ×ℕ→ℤ and take its rows. questions.theory: Finite counting rests on injective assignments, partitions, and careful tracking of possible configurations. The pigeonhole principle states that if N objects are assigned to k boxes, some box has at least ceil(N/k) objects. This conclusion guarantees existence of one crowded box, not the same occupancy in every box. The power set of an n-element set has 2ⁿ elements, since each element has two independent choices, inclusion or exclusion. An injection from a finite set to another requires the target to be at least as large; a surjection requires the domain to be at least as large. To prove a counting claim, identify the objects and boxes or construct a bijection. Counterexamples should satisfy all hypotheses and show that the stronger proposed conclusion fails.  Countability is hereditary under taking subsets. A partition of a countably infinite set into countably many nonempty parts can have all parts finite or all parts infinite. Constructing these two cases distinguishes the universal countability conclusion from unsupported size restrictions.

similar_questions.prompt: Can a countable set be partitioned into countably many infinite parts?

similar_questions.prompt: Can ℤ be partitioned entirely into finite parts?
similar_questions.solution: Yes. Enumerate 0,1,−1,2,−2,… and make each listed integer its own singleton. The parts are nonempty and finite.

Comparison with a convergent nonnegative series, the alternating-series test, and Dirichlet’s test have distinct hypotheses that must be verified. questions.prompt: F:ℝ²→ℝ² is F(x,y)=(ax+by+c,dx+ey+f), with real constants. Which hold?

options.D: F has partial derivatives of every order

hints: Separate the constant translation from the linear matrix.

questions.solution: Write F(v)=Mv+b. Its derivative is the constant matrix M, and ‖F(v)−F(w)‖≤‖M‖‖v−w‖, giving global Lipschitz and uniform continuity, hence continuity. First partial derivatives are constants and every derivative of order at least two is zero. All four statements follow.
questions.theory: Multivariable calculus studies derivatives and continuity for maps between Euclidean spaces. The total derivative at a point is a linear map approximating the function with remainder negligible compared with the input distance. Its matrix in standard coordinates is the Jacobian, assembled from first partial derivatives. Existence of partial derivatives alone does not imply differentiability; an affine map has zero remainder and therefore is differentiable everywhere. A uniform Lipschitz bound implies uniform continuity by choosing a distance tolerance independently of the points. For a square Jacobian, invertibility is equivalent to a nonzero determinant. Bijectivity of a coordinatewise map follows from bijectivity of its scalar component, whereas positivity of derivatives and mere nonvanishing derivatives must be distinguished. Higher derivatives of affine functions vanish identically. An affine map has exactly zero first-order remainder, so the total derivative exists without any limiting error.

questions.prompt: V is a nonzero finite-dimensional vector space over a finite field. Which can NEVER hold?

options.A: V is a union of two proper subspaces
options.B: V is a union of three proper subspaces

hints: Prove that the sum of a vector from each exclusive part is in neither subspace.
Use 1-dimensional spaces over F₂ and F₃ to test basis-count claims.
questions.solution: Two proper subspaces cannot cover any vector space. If neither contains the other, take u∈U\W,v∈W\U; then u+v belongs to neither. If one contains the other their union remains proper. B can hold for F₂², the union of its three 1-dimensional lines. C can hold for 1-dimensional F₂ space, whose only basis is its unique nonzero vector. D can hold for 1-dimensional F₃ space: its two nonzero vectors separately form the two bases. Thus only A is impossible.
questions.theory: A linear map is represented by a matrix once bases are chosen. Its rank is the dimension of its image and its nullity is the dimension of its kernel; the rank-nullity theorem says their sum equals the dimension of the domain. Products satisfy rank(AB)≤min(rank A,rank B). A square matrix over a field is invertible exactly when its determinant is nonzero. An eigenvector is a nonzero vector mapped to a scalar multiple of itself; the scalar is its eigenvalue. An invariant subspace is mapped into itself. Real symmetric matrices have real eigenvalues and an orthonormal eigenbasis. Positive definiteness means xᵀAx>0 for every nonzero real x. Distinguish a nonzero matrix from a nonsingular matrix, and specify the coefficient field or ring when testing invertibility.  Over a finite field, counting bases can be done by choosing linearly independent vectors successively. In one dimension each nonzero vector alone is a basis, giving exactly q−1 bases. The obstruction to covering by two proper subspaces is structural and works over both finite and infinite fields.

similar_questions.prompt: List the proper lines in F₂².
similar_questions.solution: They are {00,10},{00,01},{00,11}. Their union is all four vectors, so three proper subspaces can cover.

similar_questions.prompt: How many bases does a 1-dimensional space over F₅ have?
similar_questions.solution: Every nonzero vector alone is a basis, and there are 5−1=4 nonzero vectors, so four bases.

questions.solution: If a connected subset contained distinct points, at least one coordinate projection would be a connected subset of ℚ with two distinct values. An irrational between them separates that subset, impossible. Thus connected subsets are singletons, proving B and disproving A. The inherited Euclidean metric makes ℚ² Hausdorff, proving C. For D, the rational parametrization ((1−t²)/(1+t²),2t/(1+t²)),t∈ℚ, approaches a point on the circle with irrational coordinates when rational t tends to a suitable irrational (e.g. √2). questions.theory: Topology studies continuity and geometric structure through open sets. A subspace inherits intersections of ambient open sets. A space is Hausdorff if distinct points have disjoint neighborhoods; every metric space and its subspaces are Hausdorff. Connectedness means the space cannot be separated into two nonempty disjoint relatively open subsets. Continuous images of connected sets are connected, and connected subsets of the real line are intervals. Compactness means every open cover admits a finite subcover; in Euclidean spaces it is equivalent to closedness and boundedness. Compact subsets of a Hausdorff space are closed. A continuous inclusion sends a compact subspace set to a compact ambient set, so an ambient missing limit point disproves compactness even when the set is relatively closed. Coordinate projections need not send arbitrary closed sets to closed sets.
